description: We are Team Lyra, we are a group of friendly, enthusiastic, outgoing and curious girls, interested in challenges, coding, space and researching.
summary:
Lyra is an all-in-one health-monitoring app designed to protect astronauts throughout their space missions. It brings essential features together in one platform, making health management easier and more efficient.
One of our key features is L.E.O.N., an AI companion that assists astronauts with daily activities. We also provide personalised fitness and nutrition plans based on individual health conditions. Our calorie tracker offers three options: ISS menu, photo tracking and manual input. With photo tracking, astronauts can simply take a picture of their meals, allowing AI to estimate their calorie, protein and fat intake, as well as water consumption.
Additionally, our supply tracking system helps astronauts manage essential resources onboard. To ensure their safety, Lyra sends instant alerts with voice notifications when unusual health readings or dangerous radiation levels are detected. Our interactive 3D human anatomy also allows astronauts to better understand and monitor their bodies.
Ultimately, Lyra aims to make space missions safer, healthier and more manageable for every astronaut.
details:
Intro

Lyra is a health-monitoring app for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It brings the crew member's body, mind, medical supplies, and spacecraft environment together in one place.

How does it work

At its center is L.E.O.N., a voice-first AI companion. The astronaut says "Hey Leon", or taps the glowing round button, and a semi-transparent holographic circle appears over whatever page is open and answers in a fast, live voice. L.E.O.N. acts as flight surgeon, emergency responder, psychiatrist and companion. It can see everything the app knows, including vitals, alerts, sleep, mood, nutrition, workouts and it can open any page on request. It also keeps track of the food and medical inventory. In an emergency it gives the most urgent action first, then a few short numbered steps, then the exact supplies from the medical kit with their current quantities. When a warning pops up, L.E.O.N. also reads a short summary of it aloud, so the astronaut hears what is wrong even when they are not looking at the screen.

Around L.E.O.N., Lyra offers a live dashboard with heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, breathing and sleep, set around an interactive 3D holographic body. Tapping an organ shows its status and the risks it faces in space. Detailed charts cover the heart, lungs, bones and muscles, immune system and sleep. Alerts name the problem and clear on their own when the astronaut recovers. Lyra also tracks the hazards unique to spaceflight: radiation, isolation, altered gravity and the closed cabin environment, using real events such as the Soyuz MS-09 leak and the Artemis I radiation crossing. A multilingual setting has been integrated into the app, helping international astronauts whose first language is not English.

For emergencies, Lyra includes twelve step-by-step first-aid guides with a scenario drill, and a medical kit page that shows every supply on board, flags low or missing items and suggests the right supplies when a warning appears. Daily self-assessments and a mental wellbeing survey look after the mind. Nutrition and hydration logging from the real ISS menu, including AI analysis of a food photo, and the FitOrbit workout planner, which adapts each day's training to the astronaut's readiness, support the body. Recommended targets such as maximum heart rate, daily energy and fluids adjust to the astronaut's sex, age, height and weight. Detailed reports with graphs, a mission timeline and CSV export track progress over time. A gamified space called Lyra Galaxy rewards healthy habits with star points, streaks, ranks and badges. The demo's health readings are simulated from published ISS and NASA research, and the app gives general guidance only, never a replacement for a flight surgeon.

Benefits

On a long mission, astronauts are far from a hospital, and help from Earth can be delayed or cut off. Lyra gives the crew one place to see their whole health picture instead of separate tools, so problems are spotted early. Warnings explain exactly what is wrong and what to do next, and say which supplies to use and how many are left. Because L.E.O.N. works by voice, an astronaut can get help hands-free, even while treating someone or strapped in. The app also looks after mental health and daily habits, which matter just as much as physical health on a mission lasting months.

Intended impact
Our goal is to help astronauts stay healthy and act quickly and calmly in an emergency when the ground team cannot answer straight away. As missions go further, to the Moon and Mars, crews will need to manage more of their own care, and Lyra shows how that could work. The same ideas could also help people in other isolated places, such as Antarctic research stations, submarines, remote communities or disaster zones, where medical help is far away.

Tools and technologies
Lyra is a web app written in TypeScript with React, built with Vite and styled with Tailwind CSS. The 3D holographic body is built with three.js (WebGL) and custom shaders, and the charts use Recharts. L.E.O.N.'s live voice uses OpenAI's real-time voice model over WebRTC. The app also uses OpenAI models to analyse food photos and to read warnings aloud, and the browser's speech recognition to listen for "Hey Leon". Small serverless functions on Vercel keep the AI key secret on the server, behind a sign-in. Data is saved automatically in the browser. Our data comes from NASA technical reports and published spaceflight studies, USDA FoodData Central for food nutrients, and a real bedside-monitor recording from PhysioNet for the live heart and breathing waveforms. We used Kiro IDE, Git and GitHub to develop and share our code, and an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) to help write and test it. We tested on Windows laptops, a MacBook and phones. No special hardware is needed; the readings are simulated, so real sensors could be connected later.

Creativity
Instead of another page of charts, Lyra puts a holographic human body at the center of the screen, inspired by the futuristic displays in science fiction. L.E.O.N. is not a text chatbot: it is a live voice companion that appears as a glowing hologram, knows everything in the app, and can move around the app for the astronaut. We connected features that are usually separate: a health warning links straight to first-aid steps and to the medical kit, with the exact supplies to use. We replay real spaceflight events, such as the Soyuz MS-09 air leak and the Artemis I radiation crossing, so the app feels realistic. Lyra Galaxy turns healthy habits into a game, which helps keep astronauts motivated over a long mission.

Factors considered

Accuracy came first. Every health range and target is based on published NASA and scientific sources, and the full list is shown inside the app with links. We are open that the readings are simulated and that Lyra does not replace a doctor. We adjusted health targets and advice for men and women, because their bodies respond differently to spaceflight. For emergencies, we kept instructions short and gave the most urgent step first, because a stressed person cannot read long text. Voice control lets astronauts use the app with their hands busy. We protected the AI key with a sign-in for this demo/prototype so it cannot be misused, and we kept health data on the device. Astronauts often consist of an international crew therefore a multilingual setting has been integrated into the app. This feature helps international astronauts whose first language is not English. The app works on laptops, tablets and phones, in light and dark mode, and saves automatically, so nothing is lost if the app closes. Finally, we included mental health and motivation, because isolation and stress are among the biggest risks on long missions.
